## Definition

The Acoustic Voice Quality Index (AVQI) is an objective method to quantify the
severity of overall voice quality in concatenated continuous speech and
sustained phonation segments [@barsties2016avqi]. It is a multivariate
construct based on linear regression that combines six acoustic markers into a
single score for the whole voice sample [@barsties2016avqi]. That score
represents the overall voice quality — the hoarseness level — of the sample
[@delgado2018avqi].

The index was proposed by @maryn2010ecological and was one of the first measures to
combine both speech types [@delgado2018avqi]. The rationale for the combination:
sustained vowels are easily elicited and less affected by articulation and
dialect, while continuous speech is more representative of a patient's daily
voice [@delgado2018avqi].

## Computation

### Speech material and concatenation

The subject sustains the vowel [a:] for longer than 3 seconds, and a 3-second
mid-vowel portion is selected. The subject also reads a phonetically balanced
text aloud at comfortable pitch and loudness. For AVQI version 03.01 in Dutch,
the continuous-speech part is trimmed to the first 34 syllables of the text,
the 3-second [a:] segment is appended, and the result is saved as a single
sound file [@barsties2016avqi]. Acoustic analysis is applied only to the voiced
segments of the continuous speech — extracted by an automated Praat detection
script — plus the appended vowel segment [@barsties2016avqi].

### Component measures

All six parameters are obtained in Praat from the concatenated signal
[@barsties2016avqi; @delgado2018avqi]:

| Parameter | Definition |
|---|---|
| Smoothed cepstral peak prominence (CPPS) | Distance between the first rahmonic's peak and the point of equal quefrency on the regression line through the smoothed cepstrum — see the [CPPS chapter](cpps.qmd) |
| Harmonics-to-noise ratio (HNR) | Base-10 logarithm of the ratio between periodic energy and noise energy, × 10 |
| Shimmer local (Shim) | Absolute mean difference between amplitudes of successive periods, divided by the average amplitude |
| Shimmer local dB (ShdB) | Base-10 logarithm of the difference between amplitudes of successive periods, × 20 |
| General slope of the spectrum (Slope) | Difference between the energy in 0–1000 Hz and in 1000–10000 Hz of the long-term average spectrum |
| Tilt of the spectral trendline (Tilt) | The same difference computed on the trendline through the long-term average spectrum |

: The six AVQI components [@barsties2016avqi]. {#tbl-avqi-components}

### Regression equation (version 03.01)

As printed by @barsties2016avqi:

$$
\text{AVQI}_{03.01} = \bigl(4.152 - 0.177\,\text{CPPS} - 0.006\,\text{HNR}
- 0.037\,\text{Shim} + 0.941\,\text{ShdB}
+ 0.01\,\text{Slope} + 0.093\,\text{Tilt}\bigr) \times 2.8902
$$

The published Praat script displays the resulting score on a 0–10 axis, marked
green below the Dutch threshold of 2.43 and red above it [@barsties2016avqi].

::: {.callout-note}
## One equation, two misprints
Two validation papers print this equation differently. @barsties2020german
print the HNR term as "(0.0006-HNR)" and @delgado2018avqi as
"(0.0006 − HNR)", both with a minus sign where a multiplication is expected;
@delgado2018avqi also print the Tilt coefficient as 0.0993. The other
sources — @barsties2016avqi (text and appendix script), @englert2021avqi,
and @castillo2023avqi — give 0.006 × HNR and 0.093 × Tilt, as above. All printed forms were checked
against the publisher PDFs, so the differences are in the publications.
When implementing the index, take the coefficients from the Praat script
printed in the appendix of @barsties2016avqi rather than from an equation
retyped in a later paper.
:::

### Versions 02.02 and 03.01

In the earlier AVQI versions the analyzed continuous-speech part was much
shorter than the constant 3-second vowel part (1.53 s of voiced speech in
Dutch, 1.99 s in Japanese) [@delgado2018avqi]. Version 03.01 balances the
analyzed durations of the two speech types by expanding the continuous-speech
sample from 17–22 syllables to around 34 syllables, for higher ecological
validity and balanced internal consistency [@barsties2016avqi;
@delgado2018avqi]. Early AVQI workflows required both SpeechTool and Praat;
once CPPS was implemented in Praat, the index ran in Praat alone, with highly
comparable outcomes [@barsties2016avqi].

The regression-based combination of measures over a concatenated sample was
explored for tracheoesophageal (alaryngeal) voice by @maryn2009cepstral, where
a two-factor model combining CPP with the prominence of the second spectral
harmonic reached *r~s~* = 0.87 with listener judgments.

## What it captures

The AVQI quantifies overall voice quality as judged by the grade (G) of the
GRBAS scale — the degree of hoarseness or voice abnormality [@barsties2016avqi;
@delgado2018avqi]. Concurrent validity with mean perceptual G is strong:
*r* = 0.815 in the Dutch external validation (66.4% of variance)
[@barsties2016avqi] and *r* = 0.835 in Spanish (69.7% of variance)
[@delgado2018avqi]. CPPS is the main factor in the multivariate model
[@barsties2016avqi]. @barsties2018meta report, from the earlier
overall-voice-quality meta-analysis of Maryn, Roy et al. (2009), weighted
correlations for CPPS of 0.63 for sustained vowels and 0.88 for continuous
speech.

A previous AVQI investigation [@maryn2010avqi] reported high sensitivity to
voice changes through voice therapy [@barsties2016avqi].

## Normative data

Diagnostic thresholds separate normophonic from hoarse voices, with hoarseness
defined as mean perceptual grade G ≥ 0.5 [@barsties2016avqi]. The threshold
differs between AVQI versions and languages [@barsties2020german], so each row
states its language and pipeline. Use the row validated for the patient's
language and the AVQI version in use; see
[Pipeline Dependence and Reference Values](foundations-pipeline.qmd).

| Language | Sample | Pipeline | Threshold | Sensitivity | Specificity | AUC | Class |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dutch, external validation | 970 dysphonic, 88 normal | AVQI 03.01; Praat 5.3.57 | 2.43 | 0.785 | 0.932 | 0.923 | language-conditional |
| Spanish | 136 dysphonic, 47 normal | AVQI 03.01; Praat 6.0.22 | 2.28 | 0.748 | 0.946 | 0.905 | language-conditional |
| German | 175 dysphonic, 43 healthy; 27 syllables | AVQI 03.01; Praat 5.3.57 | 1.85 | 0.72 | 0.90 | 0.90 | language-conditional |
| French | 90 ENT patients, 30 controls; 27 syllables | AVQI 03.01; Praat version not stated; recorded at 11,025 Hz | 2.33 | 0.598 | 1.00 | 0.788 | language-conditional |
| Brazilian Portuguese | 113 dysphonic, 37 nondysphonic; counting 1–11 (17 syllables) | AVQI 03.01 script; Praat 6.0.40 | 1.33 | 0.788 | 0.906 | 0.904 | language-conditional |
| Brazilian Portuguese, counting 1–11 | 40 dysphonic, 13 healthy; 17 syllables | AVQI 03.01; Praat 6.0.06 | 1.16 | 0.86 | 0.80 | 0.87 | language-conditional |
| Brazilian Portuguese, reading text | same 53 speakers; 32 syllables | AVQI 03.01; Praat 6.0.06 | 1.56 | 0.886 | 1.00 | 0.963 | language-conditional |
| US English | 148 with voice disorders, 49 non-clinic-seeking; first 22 syllables of the Rainbow Passage | AVQI 03.01 in VOXplot 2.0.0; Praat 6.3.06 for extraction | 1.17 | 0.62 | 0.95 | 0.84 | language-conditional |
| Japanese | 455 recordings, 55 from controls; 30 syllables, time-balanced | AVQI 03.01; Praat version not stated | 2.06 | 0.721 | 0.938 | 0.915 | language-conditional |
| Persian | 136 dysphonic, 45 vocally healthy; 20 syllables, durations balanced | AVQI 03.01 in VOXplot, version not stated | 1.63 | 0.732 | 0.91 | 0.850 | language-conditional |
| Pooled: eight AVQI v03 studies (context only) | 12 languages | multiple | none; study thresholds ranged 1.33–3.15 | 0.82 | 0.92 | 0.94 (SROC) | meta-analytic |

: AVQI 03.01 diagnostic thresholds. Dutch: @barsties2016avqi; Spanish: @delgado2018avqi; German: @barsties2020german; French: @pommee2020avqi; Brazilian Portuguese: @englert2021avqi (150 speakers) and @englert2020material (53 speakers, two tasks); US English: @castillo2023avqi; Japanese: @hosokawa2019avqi; Persian: @aghajanzadeh2025persian; pooled: @jayakumar2024avqi. Praat versions for the Dutch, Spanish and German rows are those cited in each paper's reference list. {#tbl-avqi-thresholds}

The pooled row is descriptive context, not a cutoff. Its sensitivity was
highly heterogeneous across studies (*I*² = 95.3%), its specificity much less
so (*I*² = 16.4%) [@jayakumar2024avqi].

One further set of figures belongs to the Dutch internal validation, and is
not published as a second Dutch cutoff. @barsties2015consistency, the
60-sample study that produced the version 03.01 weighting, reports for its
balanced-duration condition an AROC of 0.98 at a threshold of 2.43, with
sensitivity 1.00 and specificity 0.936. These are development-sample figures:
the threshold was evaluated on the same recordings that produced the model's
weights, which is what a sensitivity of exactly 1.00 and an infinite positive
likelihood ratio indicate. The Dutch row of @tbl-avqi-thresholds therefore
carries the external validation on 1058 samples instead
[@barsties2016avqi]. Note that the secondary literature transposes the two
figures, giving sensitivity 0.936 and specificity 1.00.

The Japanese threshold needs care for a different reason, set out under
*Threshold derivation criteria* below. A separate paper by the same group
validated AVQI version **02.02** in Japanese and reports a threshold of 3.15,
with sensitivity 72.5% and specificity 95.2%, on a standardized syllable
number of 22 [@hosokawa2017avqi]. That is not a rival estimate of the 2.06 in
the table: the two belong to different versions of the index, with different
regression weights and different speech-material lengths, so 3.15 cannot be
compared with any threshold in @tbl-avqi-thresholds. Always pair an AVQI
threshold with its version.

**Threshold derivation criteria.** The thresholds in @tbl-avqi-thresholds are
not all derived the same way. The Japanese validation computed candidates from
both the Youden Index and the upper 95th percentile of its control cohort. The
Youden Index gave 1.41, with balanced sensitivity 84.4% and specificity 85.6%;
the 95th percentile gave 2.06, at 72.1% and 93.8%; and the original Dutch
threshold of 2.43 applied to the same sample gave 64.6% and 97.3%
[@hosokawa2019avqi]. The authors recommend 2.06, because at that value
sensitivity and specificity came close to what the Dutch threshold produced in
their cohort, and the table follows them [@hosokawa2019avqi]. The consequence
is that the Japanese row trades sensitivity for specificity relative to a
Youden-derived cutoff, so comparing it with the Youden-derived rows compares
two criteria and not only two languages. Some of the spread in published AVQI
thresholds is a spread of derivation methods rather than of languages.

Likelihood ratios at the optimal threshold: LR+ = 11.54, LR− = 0.23 (Dutch
external validation) [@barsties2016avqi]; LR+ = 13.85, LR− = 0.26 (Spanish,
threshold chosen by the Youden index) [@delgado2018avqi]; LR+ = 7.40,
LR− = 0.31 (German) [@barsties2020german]; LR+ = 8.38, LR− = 0.23 (Brazilian
Portuguese) [@englert2021avqi]; LR+ = 12.46, LR− = 0.40 (US English)
[@castillo2023avqi]. The LR+ values printed by @englert2020material are
below 1 or negative and cannot be correct, so they are not reproduced here.

The original AVQI, which carried no version number, reported two cutoff
options: 2.36 (sensitivity 91%, specificity 59%) and 2.95 (sensitivity 74%,
specificity 96%). The authors suggest 2.95 may be more appropriate when the
main interest is screening [@maryn2010ecological]. These values apply to that
version only.

The US English validation standardized the continuous-speech part at 22
syllables of the Rainbow Passage, recorded in a quiet environment (ambient
noise below 35 dB) with a head-mounted microphone at 44.1 kHz / 16 bit, and
computed the index in VOXplot 2.0.0, which the authors state uses established
Praat algorithms and the same equation [@castillo2023avqi]. Its threshold,
1.17, lies below the range of the AVQI
meta-analysis, whose literature search ended in July 2021
[@jayakumar2024avqi]. The authors note that other English dialects and
accents remain to be examined [@castillo2023avqi].

## Confounds and cautions

**Language-specific standardization is required.** The continuous-speech part
must be trimmed to a syllable count that yields about 3 seconds of voiced
speech, and the count differs by language: 34 syllables in Dutch, 33 in
Spanish, 30 in Japanese for AVQIv3 [@delgado2018avqi].

**Thresholds differ by language, by version, and by derivation criterion.** Reported optimal AVQI
version 03.01 cutoffs are 2.43 (Dutch), 2.28 (Spanish) and 2.06 (Japanese). The
differences are small, which may indicate that AVQI is relatively insulated
from inter-language phonetic differences [@delgado2018avqi]. The validations
since widen the spread: 1.85 German, 2.33 French, 1.33 Brazilian Portuguese,
1.63 Persian. A version 02.02 threshold sits on a different scale altogether,
as the Japanese version 02.02 value of 3.15 shows [@hosokawa2017avqi]. Nor is
a percentile-derived threshold directly comparable with a Youden-derived one,
which is the case for the Japanese row.

**Equal proportion of the two speech tasks.** Earlier work found the sustained
vowel dominating the final AVQI score more than the continuous speech.
@barsties2015consistency tested three speech-material durations against that:
17 syllables plus 3 s of sustained phonation, a customised continuous-speech
length plus 3 s, and a whole text plus 3 s. Concurrent validity was comparable
across all three (*r*~s~ 0.891 to 0.929), but precision was best, and the two
tasks' contributions balanced, in the middle condition. This is the reasoning
behind the standardized syllable count that the later validations use.

**Recording conditions matter.** Validation recordings were made in sound-
treated rooms with head-mounted condenser microphones at 44.1 kHz / 16 bit,
with environmental noise verified against a signal-to-noise norm
[@barsties2016avqi; @delgado2018avqi]. The AVQI script itself states that
reliable analysis requires optimal data-acquisition conditions
[@barsties2016avqi].

**The Praat version matters.** With the same AVQI 03.01 script and the same
218 German recordings, seven Praat versions formed three clusters. Praat
6.0.44 introduced a bug in the CPPS computation that 6.0.47 fixed. With
version 6.0.46, AVQI scores were on average 4.16 points lower, and
sensitivity at the German threshold of 1.85 fell from 72% to 23%. Across the
unaffected versions, mean differences were negligible, but single recordings
differed by up to 0.62 points [@stappenbeck2020praat]. The authors
recommend using the Praat version of the validation study for the language
in question, or checking a new version against an earlier one on test
recordings [@stappenbeck2020praat].

**Sampling rate.** The French validation recorded at 11,025 Hz
[@pommee2020avqi], so its signals contain nothing above about 5.5 kHz. The
AVQI script computes the LTAS slope and trend-line tilt over bands that reach
10 kHz [@barsties2016avqi], so two of the six components are computed on a
narrower band than in the other validations. Treat the French threshold as
applying to recordings made at that rate.

**Report the version.** Versions 02.02 and 03.01 differ in the length of the
continuous-speech part (17 vs. 34 syllables) and in the regression weighting
[@barsties2016avqi]. Report the version with every score.

**Base rates affect ROC statistics.** The Dutch external validation sample
contained 8% normophonia and 92% dysphonia; likelihood ratios were used
because they are less vulnerable to base-rate differences than ROC statistics
alone [@barsties2016avqi].

**Voicing detection is part of the pipeline.** Voiced segments of continuous
speech are extracted automatically by a Praat script before measurement
[@barsties2016avqi].

## Validation

Across 1118 subjects in two studies, AVQI 03.01 showed a homogeneous weighted
mean correlation of *r* = 0.821 with perceptual overall voice quality, against
*r* = 0.790 for the initial AVQI model pooled over 507 subjects
[@barsties2016avqi]. In the same pooled analysis, the Dysphonia Severity Index
reached a heterogeneous weighted mean *r* = 0.524 and the Cepstral Spectral
Index of Dysphonia *r* = 0.788 (sustained vowel) and 0.748 (continuous
speech); AVQI 03.01 reached the highest concurrent validity among these
multiparametric indices [@barsties2016avqi]. Language validations include
Dutch [@barsties2016avqi] and Spanish [@delgado2018avqi], with Japanese
figures reported in the latter.
